output.summary: Anti-Hu (ANNA-1) targets an intracellular antigen and is strongly associated with small cell lung carcinoma [Graus_2021]. Syndromes with antibodies to intracellular antigens respond less to immunotherapy than those with antibodies to neural surface antigens, and outcome depends largely on treatment of the tumour. Periodic discharges on the ictal-interictal continuum are classified by the clinical and EEG response to an IV antiseizure drug [Salzburg_NCSE_2015].

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the encephalopathy to alcohol withdrawal: the decline began about 2 weeks before he stopped drinking 5 days ago, and withdrawal seizures occur 6 to 48 hours after cessation.
Do not continue thiamine at 100 mg daily: deficiency with possible Wernicke encephalopathy needs treatment doses [EFNS_Wernicke_2010].
Do not use valproate: alcohol-related liver disease (AST 124, bilirubin 1.4) and platelets 138.
Do not rely on immunotherapy alone: anti-Hu syndromes need tumour-directed treatment [Graus_2021].
Do not induce anaesthetic coma for ictal-interictal continuum LPDs before the benzodiazepine trial and a second-line ASM [Brophy_2012].
required_recommendations: Give a benzodiazepine now under continuous video-EEG with bedside testing, as treatment and as the diagnostic trial for the LPDs: IV lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg (maximum 4 mg per dose, repeat once), or IM midazolam 10 mg without IV access [Glauser_2016; Salzburg_NCSE_2015].
Load a second-line ASM: IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4500 mg), and avoid valproate because of alcohol-related liver disease with thrombocytopenia [ESETT_2019].
Continue video-EEG for at least 24 hours after clinical and electrographic seizure control [Brophy_2012].

Give high-dose IV thiamine, at least 200 mg three times daily [EFNS_Wernicke_2010] (commonly 500 mg three times daily for 2 to 3 days, then 250 mg daily), with or before any dextrose, without delaying glucose [Brophy_2012].
Stop acyclovir once CSF HSV PCR is negative, given the antibody-defined alternative diagnosis [Tunkel_2008].
Start first-line immunotherapy: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 5 days, or IVIG 0.4 g/kg daily for 5 days [Graus_2016].
Arrange tissue diagnosis of the hilar mass (EBUS-guided or bronchoscopic biopsy) with oncology [Graus_2021].
Refer to oncology for tumour-directed treatment once histology is known; with anti-Hu it is the main determinant of neurological outcome [Graus_2021].

avoided_actions.rationale: No clinical suspicion of cardiac source of embolus or cardiogenic seizure; routine echo is not indicated in SE workup absent cardiac findings.
No suspicion of arrhythmogenic syncope or cardiac comorbidity precipitating SE; routine telemetry beyond standard ICU monitoring adds cost without yield.
Polysomnography studies sleep disorders and has no role in the acute evaluation of status epilepticus.

accepted: Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis (anti-Hu, suspected small cell lung carcinoma) presenting with ictal-interictal continuum evolving to non-convulsive status epilepticus after positive benzodiazepine diagnostic trial

Thiamine 42 and heavy drinking: a coexisting deficiency to treat, but it does not produce lateralized periodic discharges or mesial temporal FLAIR change

key_clinical_evidence: LPDs+F on the ictal-interictal continuum that resolve with clinical improvement during an IV benzodiazepine trial meet the Salzburg criteria for NCSE
Anti-Hu is a high-risk onconeural antibody, usually with small cell lung carcinoma; tumour diagnosis and treatment come first, and immunotherapy alone is insufficient
Alcohol withdrawal seizures occur 6 to 48 hours after cessation, not 5 days later, and do not explain a 3-week decline
The subacute 3-week decline before cessation, with mesial temporal FLAIR change and inflammatory CSF, is the limbic encephalitis timeline
A thiamine level of 42 needs treatment doses, not 100 mg daily

patient.history_present_illness: A 52-year-old White male middle school teacher was referred urgently from a community hospital neurology service after developing new-onset unresponsiveness. He had been admitted for evaluation of three days of progressive behavioral changes and word-finding difficulty. His wife reports that for three weeks he had been increasingly forgetful, getting lost on familiar routes, and last week had an episode where he stared blankly for 2 minutes with subtle lip movements — not recognized as a seizure at the time. He has no prior epilepsy. He was admitted to the outside hospital, started on IV acyclovir empirically, and transferred for continuous EEG and further work-up when he became unresponsive. He has a history of heavy alcohol use (6-8 drinks per day for 20 years) and stopped drinking abruptly 5 days ago, as his confusion worsened. Vitals on transfer: BP 148/88, HR 96, temp 37.2°C, SpO2 97%. On examination he appears to stare distantly, with slow intermittent eye deviation to the left, and subtle lip-smacking movements. He responds minimally to his name. His wife reports his baseline was completely normal 3 weeks ago. She denies any fever at home, no travel, no sick contacts, no new medications. Family history: father with Alzheimer's dementia. No family history of epilepsy. Past medical history: alcohol use disorder, alcohol-related hepatic steatosis, hypertension.
